transcript:
Meeting header:
Date: 2026-06-18
Start: 15:00 UTC
Duration: ~75 minutes
Attendees: Maya (Redwood AE), Diego (Redwood SE), Jon (Redwood SE), Sofia (CSM), Priya (Equinox), Lars (Equinox SRE), Alex (Equinox ML), Mei (Network)

Auto-summary (auto-generated, may be rough):
- Focus: unexplained p99 spikes during morning traffic window; hypothesis: cold KV cache misses combined with multi-path routing across shards + VPC egress jitter.
- Tests agreed: cold-cache synthetic run, per-shard latency aggregation, streaming vs non-streaming A/B, quantized vs fp16 latency check.
- Next steps and owners listed.

Topics: p95/p99 profiling, KV shard routing, cold-cache behavior, streaming vs non-streaming, batching tradeoffs, quantization effects at tail, VPC networking and multi-hop latency.

Transcript body:
[00:00:00] Maya: okay everyone thanks for hopping on. quick context—Equinox has seen intermittent p99 spikes in production early morning. we want to dig into where those tokens are spending time. diego and jon will run through the runtime traces then we can triage network.
[00:00:22] Priya: yep, thanks. the spikes are small but customer-visible. p95 is fine, it's p99 that jumps 2–3x for a few minutes. our incident graph correlates with low cache hit rates but not perfectly.
[00:00:40] Diego: great. i'll start with the runtime heatmap we captured. note up front: transcription may say "KV cash" later, it's KV cache.
[00:01:05] Diego: (screen share) here's a token-by-token waterfall from one noisy window, the blue bars are runtime compute, orange is wait on I/O to KV backends, green is network egress waiting. you can see several tokens with long orange tails — those are cold-cache misses.
[00:01:38] Lars: are those misses hitting a particular shard or spread?
[00:01:45] Diego: in this capture they're hitting 3 different shards but interestingly they originate from the same upstream router that's doing sticky routing. so when that router moves a subset of traffic to a different node the prefix is not warmed and we get a cold miss cascade.
[00:02:10] Alex: are we sure it's cold cache and not a serialization delay at the KV store? some of our logs show occasional high read latency at shard-7.
[00:02:21] Jon: good call. on the backend traces shard-7 had a GC pause in the minutes prior, but the distribution of tail latencies we see at p99 is wider than that single shard. there's also a network hop spike between the inference host and the KV endpoint.
[00:02:50] Mei: on the network side we had a brief routing churn with our provider between 06:48–06:52. that caused an extra 2–3 network hops for some sessions.
[00:03:10] Diego: so combined theory: sticky upstream routing caused traffic to land on hosts with cold (or not-warmed) KV prefixes, and network churn added extra RTTs converting some of the cold-miss cost into p99 explosions.
[00:03:34] Priya: that matches the timing in our telemetry. can we quantify how much of the p99 is attributable to pure compute vs KV lookup vs network?
[00:03:45] Diego: yes, here's an aggregated breakdown from the trace: median token cost is 18 ms compute + 3 ms KV lookup + 1 ms network; p99 tokens are 22 ms compute + 120 ms KV lookup + 40 ms network in the worst windows. so KV + network dominate at tail.
[00:04:15] Maya: wow ok. so even if compute is well-quantized and batched, a few cache misses with an extra hop will swamp the p99.
[00:04:30] Alex: curious about streaming vs non-streaming—do we see different tail characteristics?
[00:04:38] Jon: yes, streaming has two opposing effects: it reduces end-to-end perceived latency for successful cached prefixes because we emit tokens earlier; but at the tail, if you get a cold miss mid-stream, you often block the stream and the p99 becomes visible to user as a long pause. in non-streaming (fully buffering) you hide some token-level jitter but the end-to-end response still hits p99.
[00:05:10] Diego: in our tests streaming vs non-streaming p99 numbers: for warm-cache streaming p99 was 150 ms; for warm-cache non-streaming p99 was 180 ms; for cold-cache streaming p99 spiked to 1.2s while non-streaming cold p99 was ~950 ms. so streaming helped warm case, hurt cold-case tail.
[00:05:46] Mei: important because Equinox uses streaming for UX reasons.
[00:05:52] Priya: yes users expect tokens right away. so we need mitigation not removal.
[00:06:02] Diego: mitigation options we covered: prewarming hot prefixes, probabilistic asynchronous warming (prefetch next KV entries), routing changes to avoid sticky routers during churn, and local LRU on the inference host to absorb sudden prefix spikes.
[00:06:25] Lars: what about batching? does increasing micro-batch size help or hurt p99?
[00:06:32] Jon: batching improves throughput and median, but it increases head-of-line blocking. if one request in the batch needs a KV lookup that's slow, it drags the whole batch. Redwood's continuous batching implementation aims to avoid that by allowing partially-filled batches to proceed, but if you force rigid batch boundaries you amplify p99.
[00:06:57] Alex: so we should prefer adaptive continuous batching + prioritized urgent small batches for interactive flows.
[00:07:07] Diego: exactly. and for the cold-cache pattern we can detect a 'warming' state and put those sessions into a lightweight isolated path that doesn't block large batches.
[00:07:20] Priya: what's the cost of prewarming? we have a lot of prefixes.
[00:07:26] Diego: cost depends on hot prefix set size. we recommend tracking prefix access skew — for telecom many requests hit a small fraction of prefixes (the long-tail is smaller than you think). a 10–20% cache warming budget covering top N prefixes often removes most spikes.
[00:07:45] Mei: on VPC side we can do route pinning to keep inference hosts close to KV endpoints and reduce cross-az hops. however provider churn still causes transient path changes.
[00:07:58] Jon: also worth noting quantization interactions — Alex, you asked earlier: at p99 the difference between int8 quantized runtime and fp16 was minimal on compute portion (~1–3 ms), but quantized models can have slightly larger variance in per-token compute when dequantization paths run, and that variance adds to the tail if combined with a cold-KV wait.
[00:08:23] Alex: so quant helps cost and median, but doesn't solve cold-cache network induced p99.
[00:08:28] Diego: correct. quantization is not a cure for IO/network tail. it's complementary.
[00:08:34] Priya: are there situations where Quant plus increased batch helps p99?
[00:08:40] Jon: in pure compute-heavy workloads, yes. but in your case the p99 is dominated by IO+network, so batching/quant reduces compute fraction but leaves IO path exposed.
[00:08:55] Maya: can you two run a small experiment? produce a trace where we artificially inject cache misses and simulate extra network hop latency, then test streaming vs non-streaming/continuous batching/isolated warming path.
[00:09:07] Diego: yes. Diego: i'll prepare a script and a dockerized synthetic driver you can run in your VPC. it will replay real prefixes and toggle prewarm strategies.
[00:09:18] Priya: we'll run it overnight. can you also annotate the traces with which router the session hit?
[00:09:25] Diego: yes we can add router-id tagging if your infra emits it (Mei).
[00:09:30] Mei: we do, i'll forward the mapping table.
[00:09:34] Priya: any security concerns with sharing traces? some contain token hashes.
[00:09:40] Sofia: we will redact PII and token material; we accept hashed prefixes for correlations. we'll send our redaction checklist.
[00:09:52] Lars: what about failover routing? if a router fails and sessions are shifted, that's when we see the worst. can Redwood handle replica routing to warm copies?
[00:10:04] Diego: Redwood supports multi-replica reads and async replication warming. we can configure read-through to nearest replica and fallback policies. also automatic in-flight duplicate reads (speculative reads) for suspiciously slow KV responses is an option — issue is extra cost.
[00:10:23] Alex: how expensive is speculative read?
[00:10:27] Jon: depends on miss rate; if miss is 0.5% it's tiny. but if you speculatively duplicate every read you double DB ops. so we recommend heuristics: only spec dup when a token crosses a latency threshold or during known unstable windows.
[00:10:44] Priya: ok. what about observability — we need better per-shard p99, not just global.
[00:10:51] Diego: agreed. action: we'll drop a template dashboard with per-shard and per-router p50/p95/p99 and token heatmaps.
[00:10:58] Priya: please also add directional network hop counts and AS path on the dashboard.
[00:11:03] Mei: i can export the AS path data.
[00:11:07] Maya: quick aside — any competitors or vendor options you considered for caching?
[00:11:12] Priya: we looked at Lambda Labs and Anthropic managed inference; also an internal self-hosted memcached cluster but it was operationally heavy.
[00:11:22] Diego: note: we can run Redwood Dedicated inside your VPC which shortens the network path and gives tighter latency SLOs. Dedicated also supports local caching and prewarm hooks.
[00:11:35] Lars: cost estimate?
[00:11:37] Maya: we'll send a ballpark for Dedicated and the cost delta for enabling prewarm caches and speculative reads.
[00:11:45] Alex: back to streaming vs non-streaming — for UX maybe hybrid: stream until you hit a cache-miss threshold then silently switch to buffered mode and show a spinner.
[00:11:58] Jon: we prototyped that; user perceived latency improves and p99 tail visible to users is reduced. switching has to be seamless.
[00:12:06] Priya: good idea. can you show that in a follow-up demo?
[00:12:10] Jon: yes, that's one of the action items.
[00:12:15] Diego: quick note on instrumentation: please ensure KV client exposes per-request origin and whether response was served from memory vs disk vs remote replica. that telemetry is crucial.
[00:12:26] Mei: confirmed. our KV client has an opt-in header we can enable.
[00:12:30] Maya: wrapping up, let's recap decisions and open questions.
[00:12:35] Maya: 1) Root cause hypothesis: combined effect of cold KV misses + upstream routing churn causing extra hops. 2) Short term mitigations: prewarm top prefixes, enable speculative reads on threshold, and pin routes where possible. 3) Medium-term: consider Redwood Dedicated in-VPC to reduce hop counts and add LRU local cache. 4) Tests: synthetic cold-cache run, annotated traces, streaming vs buffered demo, quantized compute latency test.
[00:13:05] Priya: sounds right. timeline?
[00:13:09] Maya: Diego, Jon—two weeks for initial traces and synthetic scripts. Priya/Mei—one week to share topology and logs. follow-up lab week of 2026-06-29.
[00:13:21] Priya: confirmed. thanks everyone.
[00:13:25] Maya: thanks, we'll share the dashboard template and the scripts.

End of transcript.
